import Callout from "../../../components/docs/Callout.astro";
import ThemeTokens from "../../../components/docs/ThemeTokens.astro";

A theme is ordinary CSS that yapmod inserts after the app's own styles. The stable way to change the look is to set `--ym-*` tokens; plain component CSS is also allowed when a token does not cover what you need.

## The two root attributes

While a theme is active, yapmod sets two attributes on `<html>`:

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `data-yapmod-theme` | The theme `id`. Use it to scope rules that should not leak into another theme. |
| `data-yapmod-mode` | `dark` or `light`, after the [mode is resolved](/yapmod/docs/themes/loading). |

```css
:root[data-yapmod-theme="midnight-blurple"] .some-component {
  /* only while this theme is applied */
}

:root[data-yapmod-mode="light"] {
  /* only in the resolved light mode */
}
```

Target `:root` for token blocks. The attribute is on the same element, so `:root[data-yapmod-mode="dark"]` and `html[data-yapmod-mode="dark"]` are equivalent.

## Token table

These are the tokens yapmod understands, with the app variable each one feeds and the default in each mode.

<ThemeTokens />

A token with an app variable is mapped onto that variable. The yapmod-only tokens style the parts yapmod adds itself, such as the brand and release banner.

## How tokens are mapped

When the theme is applied, yapmod builds a small token layer from the stylesheet:

1. It reads `--ym-*` declarations whose names are in the table above.
2. It maps each one onto the corresponding app variable, unless the theme already sets that app variable directly.
3. It writes the defaults into a `@layer yapmod-defaults` block, so a plain rule in your theme wins without needing `!important`.
4. It places the mapping and your stylesheet last in the document.

Two extra mappings follow from existing tokens:

| App variable | Fed by |
| --- | --- |
| `--bg-side-solid` | `--ym-bg-side` |
| `--bg-floating` | `--ym-bg-float` |

Only tokens you actually set are mapped. The rest keep the app's value, so a theme can change the accent without taking ownership of every surface.

<Callout type="note" title="Two names, one result">
`--ym-bg-main: #101014` is the portable form. `--bg-main: #101014` sets the app variable directly and is respected, but it is less portable across app versions. Prefer the `--ym-*` name unless you deliberately need to bypass the mapping.
</Callout>

## A token-only theme

A complete stylesheet can be just two blocks:

```css
:root[data-yapmod-mode="dark"] {
  --ym-bg-main: #1b1c23;
  --ym-bg-elev: #22232c;
  --ym-text: #ececf1;
  --ym-accent: #5865f2;
  --ym-on-accent: #ffffff;
}

:root[data-yapmod-mode="light"] {
  --ym-bg-main: #ffffff;
  --ym-bg-elev: #ebedef;
  --ym-text: #1d1f23;
  --ym-accent: #5865f2;
  --ym-on-accent: #ffffff;
}
```

Declare only what you want to change. Missing tokens inherit the generated defaults.

## Plain CSS

Tokens cover colour and shape, not every part of the interface. Ordinary selectors work because the theme is applied to the real page:

```css
/* Scoped to the theme so it disappears when another theme is picked. */
:root[data-yapmod-theme="midnight-blurple"] .topbar {
  backdrop-filter: blur(14px);
}

:root[data-yapmod-theme="midnight-blurple"] body {
  font-family: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif;
}
```

Keep selectors narrow and scope them with `data-yapmod-theme`. Broad rules on the body or on shared containers are the most common cause of a theme that breaks dialogs or hover states.

## Modes and specificity

- A `mode: "dark"` or `mode: "light"` theme only ever sees one value of `data-yapmod-mode`, so one block is enough.
- A `mode: "both"` theme should provide both blocks. The last block in the file does not win by itself; the attribute in the selector does.
- `!important` works, but it makes the theme hard to maintain and hard for a user to override. Prefer lower specificity and theme-scoped selectors.
- The app's own theme is a separate layer of state. See [Loading and modes](/yapmod/docs/themes/loading) before relying on host selectors.

## Fonts, images and other assets

A local theme is plain CSS, so relative URLs resolve against the Yapper page, not the theme folder. That means `url("./bg.png")` will not find a file next to `theme.css`.

- Use a full `https:` URL, or a `data:` URI, for images and fonts.
- A remote asset is a network request made by the page. A theme can load its own fonts and backgrounds, but it should not depend on a server that may disappear.
- The Community build rejects `@import`, `behavior:` and backslash escapes. It allows `url()`.

<Callout type="warning" title="A theme is trusted CSS">
Local themes are not sandboxed and are not restricted to a fixed property list. A theme can hide, move or imitate interface elements. Only install a theme whose source you trust, and review a Community theme before installing it.
</Callout>

## Quantities and units

Token values are copied as written, so any valid CSS value works for the property the app uses:

```css
:root[data-yapmod-mode="dark"] {
  --ym-radius: 6px;         /* corners */
  --ym-shadow: 0 18px 60px #00000099;  /* floating surfaces */
  --ym-border: #ffffff1f;   /* hairlines */
}
```

Keep `--ym-radius` a length, `--ym-shadow` a shadow, and the colour tokens colours. yapmod does not reinterpret the values.
